title: Strong disorder equals very strong disorder for directed polymers with disorder unbounded from above
statement: Context: for the directed polymer in an i.i.d. random environment omega on Z^d with normalised partition function W_n^beta, strong disorder means W_n^beta -> 0 a.s., very strong disorder means f(beta) := lim n^{-1} log W_n^beta < 0. Theorem 3.10 (Junk-Lacoin): in d >= 3 and for bounded disorder omega, strong disorder and very strong disorder are equivalent, and weak disorder holds at the critical temperature beta_c. The source: 'One would expect that the boundedness assumption is not necessary but let us state this as a question: Question 1. Are strong and very strong disorder equivalent for unbounded disorder omega?'
status_search: WebSearch and page fetch 2026-09-08. The published version of Junk-Lacoin, 'Strong disorder and very strong disorder are equivalent for directed polymers' (arXiv 2402.02562), states in its abstract that the proof requires the environment to be bounded from above; Lacoin's publication page (fetched) lists no later paper removing that assumption, and one search summary claiming a subsequent paper removes it could not be matched to a title. The source's own acknowledgement says Junk and Lacoin settled some questions of the first arXiv version; Question 1 survives in v4. Kept open: the Gaussian environment, the most common choice, is unbounded above and is exactly the case the theorem does not cover.

attempt.method: Locate where boundedness enters and test whether a truncation argument can remove it.
attempt.result: Junk-Lacoin's argument bounds the fractional moment E[(W_n)^theta] through a change of measure that raises the environment on a sparse set of sites; an upper bound on omega is used to control the cost of the tilt uniformly. A natural reduction: truncate omega at level K, omega^K = min(omega, K); W_n^{beta,K} <= W_n^beta e^{...}? The truncated partition function is dominated by the original one (each weight is at most the original), so strong disorder for omega implies nothing directly for omega^K, and conversely very strong disorder for omega^K gives f^K(beta) < 0 but f(beta) >= f^K(beta) + (correction), with the correction lambda(beta) - lambda^K(beta) -> 0 as K -> infinity: f(beta) >= f^K(beta) - (lambda(beta) - lambda_K(beta)) where lambda_K is the log-moment generating function of the truncated law. So if the truncated very-strong-disorder free energies f^K(beta) stayed bounded away from zero uniformly in K for beta > beta_c, the limit would inherit very strong disorder. The gap is monotonicity in K: the critical point beta_c^K of the truncated model can exceed beta_c, and f^K(beta) could tend to zero as K grows for beta slightly above beta_c, so truncation only proves the equivalence for beta above lim sup beta_c^K. The question is therefore equivalent to showing beta_c^K -> beta_c as K -> infinity, i.e. continuity of the critical temperature under truncation of the environment's upper tail, which is itself open. Note that in d = 1, 2 the equivalence holds for all environments with finite exponential moments (Comets-Vargas, Lacoin), because there the fractional-moment argument is quantitative in beta rather than at the critical point.
attempt.obstruction: Continuity of beta_c under truncation of the environment is not known; the change-of-measure proof needs a uniform bound on the tilted weights, and the Gaussian tail defeats any fixed truncation level.
attempt.key_identity: f(beta) >= f^K(beta) - (lambda(beta) - lambda_K(beta)), with lambda - lambda_K -> 0 as K -> infinity.

title: Strict negativity of the derivative of the polymer free energy throughout the strong disorder regime
statement: Context: f(beta) = lim n^{-1} log W_n^beta is the (self-averaging) free energy of the directed polymer; Bates and Bates-Chatterjee prove quantitative localisation under very strong disorder plus the assumptions that f is differentiable and f'(beta) < 0; Carmona-Hu first observed the relation between the derivative of the free energy and localisation. The source: 'Question 2. Does f'(beta) < 0 hold in the whole strong disorder regime?'
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08. Junk-Lacoin (arXiv 2402.02562) prove f(beta) < 0 for all beta > beta_c (for disorder bounded above), so the strong disorder regime is (beta_c, infinity) and f is strictly negative there; nothing found about the sign of the derivative. Kept admitted for the general (non-Gaussian) environment and for the differentiability question; the Gaussian case is reduced to known results in the attempt below.

attempt.method: For Gaussian disorder, express f'(beta) through the replica overlap by Gaussian integration by parts and convexity, then combine with the Comets-Shiga-Yoshida bound (3.11) and the Junk-Lacoin theorem.
attempt.result: Let p_n(beta) = n^{-1} E log Z_n^beta where Z_n is the unnormalised partition function, so that n^{-1} E log W_n = p_n(beta) - lambda(beta) with lambda(beta) = beta^2/2 in the Gaussian case. Each p_n is convex in beta (log of a positive linear combination of exponentials of linear functions), and p_n -> p = f + lambda pointwise, so at every beta where p (equivalently f) is differentiable, p_n'(beta) -> p'(beta). Differentiating under the expectation, p_n'(beta) = n^{-1} E[ E_mu_n( sum_{i<=n} omega_{i,S_i} ) ], and Gaussian integration by parts (E[omega_{i,x} F] = E[partial F / partial omega_{i,x}], with partial mu_n(S_i = x)/partial omega_{i,x} = beta mu_n(S_i=x)(1 - mu_n(S_i=x))) gives p_n'(beta) = beta - beta n^{-1} sum_{i<=n} E[I_i], where I_i = sum_x mu_{n}(S_i = x)^2 is the replica overlap at time i (with the caveat that mu_n is the length-n polymer measure; the source's I_i uses mu_{i-1}, which changes the sum by a boundary term of order o(n) by the usual telescoping argument). Hence f'(beta) = p'(beta) - beta = - beta lim_n n^{-1} sum_{i<=n} E[I_i] at every differentiability point. The source's (3.11) states that under strong disorder, a.s. for large n, -c_1 log W_n <= sum_{k<=n} I_k, and Junk-Lacoin give -log W_n >= n |f(beta)| (1 - o(1)) a.s. for beta > beta_c. Fatou then gives lim inf n^{-1} sum_{i<=n} E[I_i] >= c_1 |f(beta)| > 0, so f'(beta) <= - beta c_1 |f(beta)| < 0 at every point of differentiability in (beta_c, infinity). Conclusion: for Gaussian disorder (bounded-above environments are excluded from the Gaussian case, so this uses the d = 1, 2 equivalence or presumes F0018 for d >= 3), Question 2 reduces to differentiability of f, which is a.e. automatic since p is convex; the content that remains is (a) differentiability of f at every beta, and (b) the non-Gaussian environment, where the integration-by-parts identity is replaced by an inequality only.
attempt.obstruction: For non-Gaussian disorder there is no exact identity linking f' to the overlap (the analogue of integration by parts produces an error term of order beta^3 that is not signed), and the identity in the Gaussian case gives f' < 0 only at points where the convex function p = f + lambda is differentiable, which is all but countably many beta.
attempt.key_identity: Gaussian disorder: f'(beta) = - beta lim_n n^{-1} sum_{i<=n} E[I_i] at differentiability points, and sum_{k<=n} I_k >= c_1 n |f(beta)| under very strong disorder.
attempt.independent_check: The integration-by-parts step is the standard one (Carmona-Hu 2002, Comets-Shiga-Yoshida); the step from convexity of p_n to convergence of derivatives at differentiability points of the limit is the classical convex-analysis lemma.

title: Matching upper bounds on the gap between the random-walk-pinning and L^2 critical temperatures
statement: Context: for continuous-time random walks S^(1), S^(rho) on Z^d with jump intensities 1 and rho > 0 and identical symmetric irreducible transition probabilities, let beta_c^RWpin and beta_2 be the random-walk-pinning critical temperature (3.21) and the L^2 critical temperature (3.13) of the corresponding partition functions. Birkner-Sun and Berger-Toninelli proved beta_c^RWpin - beta_2 >= a rho if d >= 5 (some constant a); >= a_delta rho^{1+delta} if d = 4, for any delta > 0; >= exp(-a'_delta rho^{-delta}) if d = 3, for any delta > 2. 'Question 3. Can one obtain upper bounds matching the lower bounds?'
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 (random walk pinning model critical point shift upper bound). Found no paper giving upper bounds on beta_c^RWpin - beta_2 of the stated orders; Berger-Lacoin's sharp critical-point-shift results concern the i.i.d.-disorder pinning model, not the random-walk-pinning model whose disorder is a walk trajectory. Kept open.

attempt.method: State what an upper bound on the shift needs and why the standard second-moment route is blocked.
attempt.result: beta_c^RWpin > beta_2 is proved by lowering the free energy through a change of measure on the environment (fractional moments); an upper bound on the shift requires showing that the quenched pinning partition function W_n^{beta,pin(S)} is uniformly bounded for beta up to beta_2 + (gap), i.e. that the quenched model is delocalised barely above the annealed threshold. In the i.i.d. pinning model the corresponding sharp statements come from a second moment bound on a coarse-grained partition function, which works because the disorder is independent across blocks. Here the 'disorder' is the trajectory of S^(rho), and the intersection local time sum_i 1{S^(1)_i = S^(rho)_i} has correlations along the whole path of S^(rho); the annealed model is exactly the L^2 computation E[(W^beta_n)^2], and the second moment of the quenched partition function over S^(1) given S^(rho) is E over S^(rho) of a three-walk intersection functional, whose growth rate must be compared with the annealed one. A route that fits the lower bounds' scaling: the shift should be governed by the return probability structure of the two-walk difference process, which in d >= 5 is transient with finite variance of the intersection count, in d = 4 marginal (log corrections, hence the rho^{1+delta}) and in d = 3 critical (hence the exponentially small shift); the same heuristic that yields the lower bounds via Harris-type relevance arguments predicts the upper bounds of the same order, so the conjecture implicit in the question is that the lower bounds are sharp up to the delta's.
attempt.obstruction: Second-moment methods for the quenched partition function need decorrelation across blocks of the environment, which is the trajectory of a single random walk; controlling the three-walk intersection functional that the second moment produces, uniformly near the annealed threshold, is the missing tool.
attempt.key_identity: E_S[W_n^{beta,pin(S)}] = E[(W_n^beta)^2]: the annealed pinning threshold is the L^2 threshold beta_2.

title: Fluctuations of the heavy-tailed directed polymer at fixed temperature for tail exponent alpha > 5
statement: Context: the directed polymer in d = 1 with disorder in the domain of attraction of an alpha-stable law (Assumption 3, tail exponent alpha) and inverse temperature beta_n = hat-beta n^{-gamma}; the phase diagram in (alpha, gamma) is described by the source's Theorems 5.3-5.5 (energy-dominated stable fluctuations for 1/2 < alpha < 2 and gamma >= 3/(2 alpha), variational problems below that curve, a Gaussian regime for alpha in (2,6] and gamma >= 3/(2 alpha)). 'Question 5. Derive the limiting behaviours in the rest of the phase diagram. Do Airy and KPZ asymptotics extend when gamma = 0 and alpha > 5?'
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 (heavy-tailed directed polymer KPZ fluctuations fixed temperature tail exponent). No rigorous result on n^{1/3} fluctuations for a non-integrable polymer with heavy-tailed disorder was found; the source itself records the phase diagram as incomplete. Kept open.

attempt.method: Compare the scale of the largest weight the polymer can collect with the conjectured KPZ scale, to see where the question's threshold sits.
attempt.result: Among the ~n^2 sites of the space-time box the largest disorder value is of order n^{2/alpha}; a polymer path can always route through the maximal site at an entropic cost O(1) in log Z (a moderate deviation of the walk of order sqrt(n) costs O(1)), so log Z_n has fluctuations at least of order hat-beta n^{2/alpha} from the single largest weight. KPZ fluctuations are of order n^{1/3}. Thus for gamma = 0 the extreme weights dominate whenever 2/alpha > 1/3, i.e. alpha < 6, and the KPZ scale can only be the leading one for alpha > 6; at alpha = 6 the two scales coincide and a nonstandard limit (KPZ plus an independent extreme-value contribution) is the natural guess. The source's threshold alpha > 5 does not match this count; the discrepancy suggests either that the Gaussian regime of Theorem 5.3(ii) (alpha in (2,6]) already carries the answer for 5 < alpha <= 6 at gamma slightly positive, or that the question intends alpha > 6 for gamma = 0, and this should be checked against the source's Section 5 before the row is used. For the rest of the phase diagram below the curve gamma = 3/(2 alpha) with alpha in (2, 6], the variational-problem mechanism of Theorem 5.4 predicts fluctuation exponents chi = 2 xi - 1 with xi = (1 + alpha(1 - gamma))/(2 alpha - 1) as long as the entropy functional stays finite, and a KPZ-type exponent 1/3 should take over where chi drops below 1/3.
attempt.obstruction: There is no method for KPZ fluctuations outside integrable models or the KPZ equation itself; every known route for heavy tails (Auffinger-Louidor, Dey-Zygouras, Berger-Torri) works because the extreme weights dominate and turn the problem into a last-passage percolation over a Poisson point process, precisely the mechanism that fails once alpha > 6.
attempt.key_identity: largest weight in the box ~ n^{2/alpha} versus KPZ scale n^{1/3}: crossover at alpha = 6.
attempt.independent_check: The n^{2/alpha} scale is the standard extreme-value count for n^2 i.i.d. variables with tail exponent alpha.

title: Singularity of the mean number of clusters per site for critical planar percolation
statement: Site percolation on the triangular lattice. 'Question 1. Prove that the mean number of clusters per site kappa(p) = E_p(|C|^{-1}) behaves like |1/2 - p|^{2+alpha+o(1)}, where C is the cluster at the origin and alpha = -2/3.' (The source notes that the cluster density theta, the truncated mean cluster size chi(p) = (p - 1/2)^{-gamma+o(1)} and the two-point function are known, but this quantity is not.)
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 (mean number of clusters per site exponent 2 - alpha = 8/3 rigorous). Search summaries assert the value alpha = -2/3 is 'rigorously established', but the only rigorous exponent derivations they point to (Smirnov-Werner 2001, Lawler-Schramm-Werner) list beta, nu, gamma, eta, delta and the arm exponents, not alpha; I found no paper deriving the singularity of kappa(p). Kept open.

attempt.method: Explain in what sense the statement must be read (kappa is smooth to second order) and identify the object that controls it.
attempt.result: kappa(p) = sum_n P_p(|C| = n)/n is dominated by small clusters and is an analytic function of p away from p_c; since 2 + alpha = 8/3 > 2, kappa is twice continuously differentiable at p_c and the claimed singularity is that its third derivative blows up like |p - 1/2|^{-1/3 + o(1)}, or equivalently that kappa minus its second-order Taylor polynomial at 1/2 is of order |p - 1/2|^{8/3+o(1)}. Hyperscaling heuristic: the singular part of the free energy per site scales as the inverse volume of a correlation box, xi(p)^{-2} = |p - 1/2|^{2 nu} = |p - 1/2|^{8/3} with nu = 4/3, and kappa is the percolation free energy (the number of clusters is the q -> 1 derivative of the random-cluster partition function). Derivatives of kappa are computed by Russo's formula as sums over pivotal edges of cluster-size functionals; the third derivative involves triples of pivotal sites for the event that a cluster has a given size, and the divergence |p-1/2|^{-1/3} would follow from an estimate of the form: the expected number of triples of sites that are jointly pivotal for the cluster of the origin having size in [n, 2n], summed against 1/n, is of order xi^{-2} times (xi^2)^{...}. Concretely one needs the three-point 'pivotal' density at criticality: the probability that three sites at mutual distance r are all four-arm points of the same cluster scales like r^{-3 * 5/4} times the cluster-connection factor, and summing over scales up to xi gives the |p-1/2|^{-1/3}. So the conjecture reduces to a quantitative multi-point four-arm estimate plus a control of the analytic part; the first ingredient exists in the form of arm exponents with o(1) errors, which is insufficient because the third derivative is a difference of terms of equal size and o(1) errors in exponents destroy cancellations.
attempt.obstruction: The singularity sits in the third derivative and is of smaller order than the analytic background; extracting it needs multi-point arm estimates up to constants, and even the one-arm probability is only known up to constants in special cases (Du-Gao-Li-Zhuang 2024 for j > 1).
attempt.key_identity: kappa singular part ~ xi(p)^{-d} with xi ~ |p - p_c|^{-4/3}, i.e. 2 - alpha = d nu = 8/3.

title: Monochromatic arm exponents for critical planar percolation with three or more arms
statement: 'Interestingly, the critical exponent for j != 1 disjoint arms of the same color is not equal to the polychromatic arms exponent [Beffara-Nolin]. A natural open question is to compute these exponents: Question 2. Compute the monochromatic exponents.'
status_search: WebSearch and abstract fetch 2026-09-08. Nolin, Qian, Sun and Zhuang, 'Backbone exponent for two-dimensional percolation' (arXiv 2309.05050) derived the monochromatic two-arm (backbone) exponent exactly: a transcendental root of an elementary equation, numerically 0.3566, via the SLE bubble measure and Liouville quantum gravity. Their 2024-2025 note arXiv 2410.06419 reports the same exponent and an annulus crossing formula; its abstract says nothing about j >= 3. So Question 2 is settled for j = 2 and, as far as I could determine, open for every j >= 3. Admitted for j >= 3 only.

attempt.method: Record the structure of the j = 2 solution and identify what changes for j >= 3.
attempt.result: The polychromatic exponents come from the SLE_6 description of a single interface: j alternating arms across an annulus correspond to a boundary/interior conformal-field-theory weight computable by the Lawler-Schramm-Werner locality argument, giving the rational values (j^2 - 1)/12. Monochromatic arms are not a property of one interface; the two-arm case became tractable when Nolin-Qian-Sun-Zhuang expressed the event 'two disjoint black paths cross the annulus' through the SLE_6 bubble measure (the outer boundary of the cluster) and computed the resulting quantity with the LQG/Liouville CFT integrability, the transcendence of the answer reflecting that the exponent is not a Kac weight. For j >= 3 monochromatic arms the event involves the joint law of several nested boundary loops of one cluster: the natural object is the CLE_6 description, and the exponent should be an eigenvalue of a transfer-type operator on annulus configurations with j non-crossing monochromatic paths. What one can say without new tools: Beffara-Nolin's inequalities alpha_j^poly < alpha_j^mono < alpha_{j+1}^poly hold for all j, and the j-th monochromatic exponent is at least the backbone exponent plus the polychromatic (j-2)-arm ... more precisely the monotonicity alpha_j^mono >= alpha_{j-1}^mono + c for a positive c by an arm-separation argument. The obstruction is that the LQG computation for the backbone used the special structure of the two-arm event as a bubble (a single loop of the CLE separating inside from outside); for j >= 3 one needs the law of several loops jointly, for which no Liouville integrability formula is available.
attempt.obstruction: No conformal-field-theory prediction exists for monochromatic j-arm exponents with j >= 3, and the LQG/Liouville approach that solved j = 2 relies on a single-bubble structure that the j >= 3 events do not have.
attempt.key_identity: alpha_j^poly < alpha_j^mono < alpha_{j+1}^poly (Beffara-Nolin), with alpha_2^mono = 0.3566... transcendental (Nolin-Qian-Sun-Zhuang).

title: Arm probabilities up to constants for the planar one-arm and monochromatic events
statement: 'Even the existence of the exponents in the discrete model is not completely understood, because we miss estimates up to constants: Question 3. Refine the error term in the arm probabilities from (n/N)^{alpha_j+o(1)} to (n/N)^{alpha_j} Theta(1).' (Site percolation on the triangular lattice; the source cites a half-plane result of Mendelson-Nachmias-Watson as a step.)
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08. Du, Gao, Li and Zhuang, 'Sharp asymptotics for arm probabilities in critical planar percolation' (Comm. Math. Phys. 405 (2024) 182, arXiv 2205.15901) derive sharp asymptotics for half-plane j-arm events (j >= 1) and planar polychromatic j-arm events with j > 1, 'answering a large part of a question posed by Schramm at ICM 2006'. Their abstract excludes the planar one-arm event (j = 1) and does not mention monochromatic events. Admitted for the residual cases: the planar one-arm probability P(0 <-> distance N) = N^{-5/48} Theta(1) and the monochromatic arm events. The Codex tree already holds this paper as a status reference (sharp_arms_2022); no row there states the residual as a problem.

attempt.method: Explain why the one-arm case resists the method that handled j > 1.
attempt.result: The Du-Gao-Li-Zhuang method couples the discrete arm event to the SLE_6/CLE_6 continuum description and uses quasi-multiplicativity plus a coupling of the configuration in nested annuli to show that the ratio P(A_j(n,N)) / (n/N)^{alpha_j} converges; for j > 1 the arms fix the interface(s) crossing the annulus, and the exploration process gives a Markovian structure across scales. For the one-arm event the relevant object is the outer boundary of the cluster of the origin, which is not an exploration path from the boundary; the natural continuum object is the CLE_6 loop surrounding the origin, and up-to-constants control needs a coupling between the discrete cluster boundary and that loop with a rate of convergence at every scale, which is not available (the known convergence of the percolation exploration to SLE_6 has no quantitative rate on the full-plane loop ensemble). A weaker route: P(A_1(n, N)) is decreasing in N and quasi-multiplicative, so N^{5/48} P(A_1(1,N)) is bounded above and below by positive constants times a slowly varying function; Theta(1) is exactly the assertion that this slowly varying factor is bounded, equivalently that the ratios P(A_1(2^k, 2^{k+1}))/2^{-5/48} converge to 1 fast enough to have a convergent product, i.e. sum_k |log(2^{5/48} P(A_1(2^k, 2^{k+1})))| < infinity. That is a rate-of-convergence statement for a single-scale crossing probability, which is what the quantitative Cardy formula (Binder-Chayes-Lei, Mendelson-Nachmias-Watson) provides for half-plane events but not for the full-plane one-arm event.
attempt.obstruction: A polynomial rate of convergence for the one-arm probability at a single scale would suffice, and no rate is known for full-plane events; the monochromatic cases additionally lack an exploration-path description altogether.
attempt.key_identity: Theta(1) for the one-arm event is equivalent to summability over dyadic scales of log(2^{5/48} P(A_1(2^k, 2^{k+1}))).

title: Crossing estimates for critical percolation on every planar lattice
statement: 'Note that proofs of crossing estimates (Corollary 2.3) often invoke some symmetry (rotational invariance for instance) as well as strict planarity, but neither of these seem to be absolutely needed. A proof valid for lattices without one of these properties would be of great significance: Question 6. Prove crossing estimates for critical percolation on all planar (and possibly quasi-isometric to planar) lattices.'
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08. Kohler-Schindler and Tassion, 'Crossing probabilities for planar percolation' (Duke Math. J. 172 (2023), arXiv 2011.04618) prove a general RSW theorem for any percolation measure on the plane that is invariant under the symmetries of Z^2 (translations, rotations, reflections) and satisfies positive association, with no self-duality or independence assumption; Tassion's Voronoi RSW and the s-embedding results for FK-Ising extend the class further. None of these covers a planar lattice with only translation symmetry (no rotation or reflection), nor quasi-planar graphs, so the question as stated is not settled. Admitted with that residual.

attempt.method: Separate the two ingredients (the symmetry the general RSW uses, and planarity) and say what fails without each.
attempt.result: Kohler-Schindler-Tassion's argument needs a symmetry that exchanges the horizontal and vertical directions (to compare crossing probabilities of a rectangle and its transpose) and positive association (to glue crossings). For a translation-invariant planar lattice without a rotation, one can still define the critical point p_c and the dual lattice, and duality gives P_p(horizontal crossing of an n x m rectangle) + P_{1-p}(dual vertical crossing) = 1 up to boundary effects; at p = p_c self-duality is unavailable and the two directions may have different critical crossing behaviour, which is exactly what happens for anisotropic models (Grimmett-Manolescu's star-triangle work shows the box-crossing property survives anisotropy on the three regular lattices only because of the star-triangle transformation). A lattice-independent route would be: (i) prove that at p_c the probability of crossing an n x n box in the easy direction is bounded below (this follows from duality: one of the two directions has probability >= 1/2 at p_c by symmetry between primal and dual at the self-dual point, but a general lattice has no self-dual point, and (ii) show that a lower bound in one direction at one aspect ratio propagates to the other direction; (ii) is where the rotation symmetry is used and where the general argument stops. So the question reduces to a 'direction-exchange' lemma at criticality without symmetry: showing that if P_{p_c}(horizontal crossing of n x 2n) is bounded below then so is the vertical one. A possible mechanism is the sharp-threshold / OSSS approach: if vertical crossings were rare at p_c the model would look subcritical in one direction and supercritical in the other, contradicting the existence of a single critical point (Duminil-Copin-Raoufi-Tassion), which gives box-crossing at p_c for translation-invariant lattices with positive association up to a loss of constants that depends on the aspect ratio, but the argument I sketch is not complete: the sharpness proof gives exponential decay below p_c and a positive density above, not a bound on crossings at p_c itself.
attempt.obstruction: Without a symmetry exchanging the two axes there is no way known to compare horizontal and vertical crossing probabilities at p_c; the quasi-planar (quasi-isometric to planar) case lacks even the duality that gives one easy direction.
attempt.key_identity: duality: horizontal primal crossing and vertical dual crossing of a rectangle are complementary events.

title: Wilson's area law for four-dimensional non-Abelian lattice gauge theory at all couplings
statement: Problem 4.1 (Area law). Take any compact non-Abelian Lie group G contained in U(N) for some N >= 2 and consider any infinite volume limit of four-dimensional lattice gauge theory with gauge group G at inverse coupling strength beta. Let gamma_{R,T} be a rectangular loop of breadth R and length T in the lattice. Prove that |<W_{gamma_{R,T}}>| <= C(beta) e^{-c(beta) R T}, where C(beta) and c(beta) are positive constants that depend only on the inverse coupling strength beta and the gauge group. (The source: known at small beta by Osterwalder-Seiler; known for U(1) in three dimensions at all beta by Gopfert-Mack; the solution for four-dimensional non-Abelian theories at large beta 'remains elusive'.)
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 (area law lattice gauge theory large beta non-abelian proof). Nothing beyond the results the source lists; Chatterjee's later rigorous work (large-N Wilson loops at strong coupling, Ising lattice gauge theory) and the stochastic-quantisation constructions of Chandra-Chevyrev-Hairer-Shen in two and three dimensions do not touch the large-beta area law in four dimensions. Kept open.

attempt.method: Identify what any proof must use, from the U(1) counterexample.
attempt.result: Guth and Frohlich-Spencer showed that four-dimensional U(1) lattice gauge theory has a perimeter law at large beta, so any proof of the area law must use non-commutativity of G in an essential way; expansions in 1/beta (spin-wave/perturbative) are blind to it, because the Gaussian fluctuations around the trivial vacuum look the same for U(1) and SU(N) at the level of quadratic forms. The known small-beta proof is a cluster expansion: the Wilson loop expectation is a sum over surfaces spanning the loop weighted by beta^{area}, dominated by the minimal surface, whence e^{-c(beta) RT} with c(beta) ~ -log beta. At large beta the physical mechanism is asymptotic freedom: the effective coupling at scale L grows like 1/(b_0 log L), so at scales L(beta) ~ exp(c beta) the theory is again strongly coupled and the cluster expansion at that scale gives an area law with string tension sigma(beta) ~ L(beta)^{-2}. A rigorous version would need a block-spin renormalisation flow from beta to a strong-coupling regime, which is Balaban's program; Balaban's results control the flow (ultraviolet stability, existence of the continuum limit in a weak sense) but not Wilson loop expectations at scales beyond the correlation length. So the reduction is: area law at all beta follows from (a) a renormalisation-group map showing that the theory at coupling beta on scale L(beta) is dominated by a strong-coupling effective theory, and (b) the small-beta area law for that effective theory with an error term summable over the RG steps. Neither (a) nor (b) is available; also note that the constant c(beta) must decay like exp(-2 c' beta), which no perturbative bound can produce.
attempt.obstruction: There is no rigorous renormalisation-group control of four-dimensional non-Abelian gauge theory at the scale of the confinement length, and any mechanism must distinguish SU(N) from U(1), which excludes every expansion around the Gaussian vacuum.
attempt.key_identity: string tension prediction: sigma(beta) ~ exp(-const * beta) from asymptotic freedom, versus sigma(beta) ~ -log beta from the strong-coupling expansion.

title: Mass gap for four-dimensional non-Abelian lattice gauge theory at every coupling
statement: Problem 5.1 (Mass gap). Take any compact non-Abelian Lie group G contained in U(N), N >= 2, and any infinite volume limit of four-dimensional lattice gauge theory with gauge group G at inverse coupling strength beta. For each x in R^4 let p_x be the plaquette closest to x, and let f_beta(x) be the correlation between W_{p_0} and W_{p_x} as in (5.1) (covariance of the two plaquette variables). Show that for any beta > 0 there exists xi(beta) in (0, infinity) such that lim_{|x| -> infinity} log f_beta(x) / |x| = -1/xi(beta). Moreover, prove that lim_{beta -> infinity} xi(beta) = infinity.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08. This is the lattice formulation of the Yang-Mills mass gap; exponential decay is known at small beta by cluster expansion (Osterwalder-Seiler), and nothing is known at large beta. Chatterjee-Jafarov (2016, 'The 1/N expansion for SO(N) lattice gauge theory at strong coupling') and later large-N work stay at small beta. Kept open.

attempt.method: Reduce the two claims to properties of the transfer matrix and relate the second to the area law.
attempt.result: By reflection positivity (Osterwalder-Seiler) the lattice theory has a positive transfer matrix T on the physical Hilbert space, and plaquette correlations in a lattice direction decay like ||T^{|x|}|| restricted to the orthogonal complement of the vacuum, so the existence of the limit in the statement for x along a coordinate axis, with -1/xi = log(spectral radius of T on the vacuum's orthogonal complement), follows once one knows the spectrum of T has a gap below 1; the first claim is therefore equivalent to a spectral gap of T for all beta plus an isotropy statement (the same exponential rate in all directions, which by Osterwalder-Seiler-type arguments reduces to lattice rotation invariance of the correlation length, not automatic on the lattice but expected). So the problem is: gap(T_beta) > 0 for every beta. At small beta the gap is of order -log beta by cluster expansion. The second claim, xi(beta) -> infinity, is the statement that the gap closes as beta -> infinity, which is what makes the continuum limit possible; heuristically xi(beta) ~ exp(c beta) by asymptotic freedom. A lower bound xi(beta) >= c' beta^{1/2}... one can prove xi(beta) -> infinity? Not obviously: by Griffiths-type comparison one cannot compare non-Abelian theories at different beta monotonically. A concrete partial target: prove that the plaquette-plaquette correlation at distance |x| = 1 is bounded below by a positive constant uniformly in beta (true, by the explicit small-fluctuation Gaussian approximation at large beta), while the mass gap statement needs decay at every scale, so no scale-one computation can reach it.
attempt.obstruction: Nothing controls the transfer matrix spectrum at large beta; the problem is equivalent to the confinement/mass-gap Millennium question in its lattice form, and the only rigorous tool beyond small beta (Balaban's RG) does not produce correlation decay.
attempt.key_identity: correlation decay rate along an axis = -log of the spectral radius of the transfer matrix on the orthogonal complement of the vacuum.

title: Continuum limit of rectangular Wilson loop expectations in four-dimensional non-Abelian lattice gauge theory
statement: Problem 5.2 (Continuum limit). Take any compact non-Abelian Lie group G contained in U(N), N >= 2, and any infinite volume limit of four-dimensional lattice gauge theory with gauge group G at inverse coupling strength beta. Let gamma_{R,T} denote a rectangular loop of length T and breadth R. Prove that as beta -> infinity, there are sequences epsilon = epsilon(beta) -> 0 and c = c(beta) -> infinity, and a nonzero constant d, such that for any R and T, log <W_{gamma_{R/epsilon, T/epsilon}}> = -c (R + T) - d R T + o(1). (5.2) (The source adds that it is not clear whether the renormalisation term c(R+T) is necessary.)
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08. No rigorous construction of a four-dimensional Yang-Mills continuum limit with nontrivial Wilson loops exists (the source's Section 6 reviews Balaban's ultraviolet stability and the two- and three-dimensional constructions; Chandra-Chevyrev-Hairer-Shen's 2020-2022 stochastic quantisation constructs the 2D and 3D measures locally). Kept open.

attempt.method: Make the statement quantitative through the lattice string tension and the perimeter term, and test the o(1).
attempt.result: Write, for fixed beta, log <W_{gamma_{r,t}}> = -sigma(beta) r t - mu(beta)(r + t) + O(1) for large r, t (this is the conjectured shape combining the area law with a perimeter term coming from the self-energy of the loop; the perimeter term exists at every beta and is of order beta^{-1}... in the Gaussian approximation mu(beta) ~ C/beta). Substituting r = R/epsilon, t = T/epsilon, (5.2) requires d = sigma(beta) epsilon^{-2} + o(1) and c(beta) = mu(beta)/epsilon(beta), so the statement is equivalent to: the lattice string tension satisfies sigma(beta) = d epsilon(beta)^2 (1 + o(1)) for a suitable epsilon(beta) -> 0, and the perimeter coefficient is o(epsilon)... no, c = mu/epsilon -> infinity is allowed and expected. The content is thus (i) existence of a string tension sigma(beta) > 0 at every beta (Problem 4.1, F0026) and (ii) that sigma(beta) -> 0 as beta -> infinity in a way that makes epsilon(beta) := (sigma(beta)/d)^{1/2} the correct lattice spacing for every other observable too, in particular that the perimeter coefficient scales as mu(beta) = c(beta) epsilon(beta) with the o(1) error uniform over rectangles. The o(1) is the strongest part: it asserts that corrections to the area-plus-perimeter law (e.g. the Luscher term -(pi/12)(T/R) predicted by effective string theory for T >> R) vanish in the limit, which is false if the Luscher term is real: -pi T/(12 R) is scale invariant and would survive as a nonzero correction for fixed R, T. So the conjecture as stated, with o(1) uniformly in R, T, is in tension with the effective-string prediction; the corrected statement would read -c(R+T) - dRT + F(R,T) + o(1) with F the (conjecturally universal) scale-invariant string correction. This is a concrete reason to expect (5.2) to need modification rather than proof.
attempt.obstruction: Beyond the unproven area law, the exact form of the subleading terms of Wilson loops in the continuum is not settled even in physics; a scale-invariant Luscher-type correction would contradict the o(1) in (5.2).
attempt.key_identity: d = lim sigma(beta)/epsilon(beta)^2 and c(beta) = mu(beta)/epsilon(beta): (5.2) is a scaling statement for the lattice string tension and perimeter coefficient.
attempt.independent_check: The Luscher term -pi (d-2) T/(24 R) for a rectangular loop in d = 4 is the standard effective-string prediction (quoted from memory, not verified here).

title: Toppling-probability exponent for the Abelian sandpile in dimensions two to four
statement: Let nu be the infinite-volume stationary sandpile measure on Z^d, add a particle at the origin o, and let Av_o be the set of vertices that topple. Theorem 3.6 (Jarai-Redig-Saada): for d >= 5, c|x|^{2-d} <= nu[x in Av_o] <= C|x|^{2-d}. Conjecture 3.7. For 2 <= d <= 4 there exists eta = eta(d) >= 0 such that nu[x in Av_o] = |x|^{-(d-2+eta)+o(1)} as |x| -> infinity. (The source: upper bounds on eta in d = 2, 3, 4 were proved by Bhupatiraju-Hanson-Jarai.)
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08. Bhupatiraju, Hanson and Jarai, 'Inequalities for critical exponents in d-dimensional sandpiles' (EJP 2017) give bounds; Hutchcroft's 'Universality of high-dimensional spanning forests and sandpiles' (2018) settles d > 4 (eta = 0 with the exact exponent); a 2026 arXiv paper on tail exponents of the three-dimensional uniform spanning tree and sandpile (2605.19419) reports three-dimensional avalanche exponents, which may settle d = 3 for the radius/size exponents but I did not read it for the toppling probability. Kept open for d = 2, 3, 4 with that lead.

attempt.method: Use Dhar's formula and the wave decomposition to bound eta from both sides in terms of uniform spanning tree quantities.
attempt.result: Dhar's formula gives E_nu n(o,x) = G(o,x) ~ c|x|^{2-d} for d >= 3, so by Markov nu[x in Av_o] <= C|x|^{2-d} and eta(d) >= 0 in d = 3, 4; in d = 2 the Green function of the box diverges and Markov gives nothing, which is the source's own remark. Lower bound via the first wave: the first wave started at o is, by the Ivashkevich-Ktitarev-Priezzhev bijection, the component of o in a uniform two-component spanning forest with o and the sink in different components, and x belongs to it iff x lies in the same component as o; in the infinite-volume limit this is the event that in the wired uniform spanning forest the path from x to infinity passes through o... more precisely that x is a descendant of o. In d = 2 the probability that the LERW from x to infinity (the USF path) passes through a given point at distance r scales as r^{-(2 - 5/4)} = r^{-3/4}, by the LERW dimension 5/4 (Lawler-Schramm-Werner; Beneš-Lawler-Viklund for the point-hitting probability up to constants), so nu[x in Av_o] >= nu[x in first wave] = |x|^{-3/4+o(1)} in d = 2, giving eta(2) <= 3/4. Conjecture 3.7 in d = 2 therefore says that later waves do not change the exponent: the number of waves is n(o,o), whose mean is infinite in d = 2, but the k-th wave is the component of o in a forest conditioned on the previous waves, and a positive answer amounts to showing that the probability that x is reached by some wave is |x|^{-3/4+o(1)}, i.e. eta(2) = 3/4 = 2 - dim(LERW). In d = 3 the same reasoning gives eta(3) <= 2 - ... the LERW dimension in 3D is beta_3 = 1.624 (Kozma; Li-Shiraishi), and the descendant probability decays like r^{-(3 - beta_3)} = r^{-1.376}, so d - 2 + eta <= 1.376 gives eta(3) <= 0.376; in d = 4 the LERW has dimension 2 with logarithmic corrections, so eta(4) = 0 up to logarithms, consistent with d = 4 being critical. So the conjecture reduces to: the toppling probability has the same exponent as the first-wave probability, and the latter's exponent is d - dim(LERW_d).
attempt.obstruction: Later waves are components of spanning forests conditioned on earlier waves, a dependence for which no monotonicity or domination by the first wave is known; in d = 2 the expected number of waves is infinite, so a union bound over waves fails.
attempt.key_identity: nu[x in first wave] = P(x is a descendant of o in the wired USF) = |x|^{-(d - dim LERW_d) + o(1)}.
attempt.independent_check: The d = 2 exponent 3/4 uses dim(LERW_2) = 5/4; the d = 3 value 1.624 is Wilson's numerical estimate consistent with Li-Shiraishi's rigorous dimension (quoted from memory).

title: Existence of avalanche-size exponents for the Abelian sandpile in low dimensions
statement: Conjecture 3.8. For all d >= 2 there exist exponents tau = tau(d), tau' = tau'(d) >= 0 depending on d such that nu[S_o >= k] = k^{1-tau+o(1)} and nu[|Av_o| >= k] = k^{1-tau'+o(1)} as k -> infinity, where S_o is the total number of topplings and |Av_o| the number of toppled vertices when a particle is added at the origin under the stationary measure nu. (The source: tau <= 2 since E S_o = infinity; Manna's numerics suggest tau = tau'; Priezzhev's heuristic tau = tau' = 3/2 for d > 4 was proved by Hutchcroft.)
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08. Hutchcroft (2018) proved tau = tau' = 3/2 for d > 4 (and more generally on transitive graphs satisfying his conditions); Bhupatiraju-Hanson-Jarai give inequalities in d = 2, 3, 4; the 2026 arXiv preprint 2605.19419 on tail exponents of the 3D UST and sandpile reports exponents in three dimensions (abstract read in a search summary: avalanche size and topplings have exponent 1/3, radius exponent 1, in d = 3), which if confirmed settles d = 3. Kept open for d = 2 and 4, and d = 3 pending a read of that preprint.

attempt.method: Relate the size exponents to the radius exponent and the toppling exponent through the wave decomposition, to see that only one new exponent is really conjectured.
attempt.result: If the radius exponent alpha of Conjecture 3.9 and the toppling exponent eta of Conjecture 3.7 exist, a scaling heuristic gives the size exponents: an avalanche of radius r has |Av_o| ~ r^{d_A} for the avalanche dimension d_A and S_o ~ r^{d_A + zeta} where zeta accounts for the mean number of topplings per toppled vertex in a large avalanche, so nu[|Av| >= k] ~ nu[rad >= k^{1/d_A}] = k^{-alpha/d_A}, giving tau' = 1 + alpha/d_A and tau = 1 + alpha/(d_A + zeta). Sum rules: E S_o = infinity forces tau <= 2; Dhar's formula E n(o,x) = G(o,x) integrated over |x| <= r gives E[S_o restricted to radius r] ~ r^2 in every d (Exercise 3.4(ii) of the source), which is the constraint sum over scales r^{2 - ...}... concretely r^{d_A + zeta} nu[rad ~ r] ~ r^2 ... yields d_A + zeta - alpha = 2, a relation among the exponents that must hold if they exist. In d = 2 the first-wave picture (F0029) suggests d_A is the dimension of the component of a two-component spanning forest, plausibly 2 - o(1) with logarithmic corrections, and zeta > 0 from multiple waves. The conjecture that the exponents EXIST is weaker than computing them and would follow from a scaling-limit statement for a single wave (the USF component in a box), which in d = 2 is a question about the scaling limit of the two-component spanning forest, an object whose limit is described by SLE_8/CLE-type curves (Lawler-Schramm-Werner UST convergence) but whose component-size tail has not been computed.
attempt.obstruction: Existence of an exponent needs either a regularity property (quasi-multiplicativity across scales for avalanches, which fails because avalanches are not monotone in the configuration) or a scaling limit for waves; neither is available in d = 2, and in d = 4 logarithmic corrections make the o(1) delicate.
attempt.key_identity: d_A + zeta - alpha = 2 from Dhar's formula summed over a ball, if the exponents exist.

title: Existence of the avalanche radius exponent for the Abelian sandpile in dimensions two to four
statement: Conjecture 3.9. For all d >= 2 there exists alpha >= 0 such that nu[rad(Av_o) > r] = r^{-alpha+o(1)} as r -> infinity. When d > 4, it was conjectured by Priezzhev that alpha = 2; this has recently been proved by Hutchcroft. Upper bounds on the exponent alpha in d = 2, 3, 4 and lower bounds in d = 3, 4 were given by Bhupatiraju-Hanson-Jarai.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08. As for F0030: Hutchcroft settles d > 4; arXiv 2605.19419 (2026) reports a radius exponent 1 in d = 3 (search summary only). Open in d = 2 and d = 4; d = 3 pending verification of that preprint. Kept admitted for those dimensions.

attempt.method: Bound alpha from both sides by wave and Green-function arguments.
attempt.result: Upper bound on the tail (lower bound on alpha): rad(Av_o) > r implies some vertex at distance r topples, so nu[rad > r] <= sum_{|x| = r} nu[x in Av_o] <= C r^{d-1} r^{2-d} = C r in d >= 3 by Dhar-Markov, which is useless (exceeds 1); the better bound uses that the avalanche is connected and contains a path from o to distance r, so nu[rad > r] <= nu[first wave or later waves reach distance r] and the first wave reaching distance r is the event that the USF component of o in the two-component forest has radius r, i.e. that o has a descendant at distance r, which has probability r^{-(d - dim LERW)}... no: a descendant at distance r means the USF path from some x at distance r passes through o, probability r^{d-1} * r^{-(d - dim LERW)} = r^{dim LERW - 1}, which is >= 1 for dim LERW >= 1: so union bounds fail, and one must use the exact structure: the first wave has radius > r iff the bush of o (the set of descendants) reaches distance r; in the 2D USF the descendant set of a point is finite with a tail that can be computed from the LERW: P(bush of o has radius > r) = r^{-alpha_1 + o(1)} with alpha_1 = 2 - dim LERW = 3/4 in d = 2 (the bush reaching distance r forces the LERW from some far point to pass through o and then the point's path... this equals the one-arm-type exponent of the UST which is known to be 3/4? I have not verified this value; it is the natural guess). Then alpha(2) <= 3/4 if later waves have radius at most comparable to the first. For d = 4, the source notes dim LERW = 2 with log corrections and Hutchcroft's alpha = 2 above four dimensions, so alpha(4) = 2 with logarithms is the natural conjecture, and the o(1) in the exponent hides the logarithmic factor. The existence question therefore reduces, as in F0029/F0030, to comparing the radius of the full avalanche with the radius of its first wave.
attempt.obstruction: Later waves are not dominated by the first; no regularity across scales is known for the avalanche radius in d <= 4, and in d = 2 even the exact first-wave radius exponent has to be extracted from the UST scaling limit.
attempt.key_identity: first wave = component of o in a uniform two-component spanning forest separating o from the sink (Ivashkevich-Ktitarev-Priezzhev).

title: Logarithmic corrections in the two-point correlations of heights 1, 2, 3 in the two-dimensional sandpile
statement: Poghosyan, Grigorev, Priezzhev and Ruelle showed that for the two-dimensional Abelian sandpile, nu[eta(o) = 0, eta(y) = h] - p(0)p(h) = (c_h log|y| + d_h)/|y|^4 + O(|y|^{-5}) for h = 1, 2, 3, with explicit non-zero constants. Piroux and Ruelle predicted, from logarithmic conformal field theory, that nu[eta(o) = h_1, eta(y) = h_2] - p(h_1)p(h_2) ~ c_{h_1,h_2} (log^2 |y|)/|y|^4 as |y| -> infinity for h_1, h_2 in {1, 2, 3}. Open Question 5.19. Show that the correlation between heights 1, 2, 3 is of order (log^2 |y|)/|y|^4.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08. The Poghosyan-Grigorev-Priezzhev-Ruelle computation (J. Stat. Mech. 2010, arXiv 1005.2088) covers the (0, h) correlations; a search summary mentions later work revisiting height correlations with Kenyon-Wilson's connection/defect-line technique, without a claim that the (h_1, h_2) log^2 asymptotics has been proved. Durre's rigorous results concern the height-0 (minimal height) field. Kept open.

attempt.method: Explain the source of the logarithms via the Majumdar-Dhar/Priezzhev representation, and why the h >= 1 case is harder.
attempt.result: Height 0 at a vertex is a local event for the uniform spanning tree under the burning bijection (the vertex is a leaf in a specific sense), so nu[eta(o) = 0, eta(y) = 0] is a finite determinant of the Green function differences and decays as |y|^{-4} without logarithms (Majumdar-Dhar). Heights h >= 1 are not local in the tree: by Priezzhev's computation the probability p(h) involves the probability that a vertex has a given number of predecessors, expressed through spanning forests with a nonlocal 'theta-graph' constraint whose weight is the derivative of a determinant with a defect line, and the logarithm arises because the relevant two-component spanning forest probabilities involve the potential kernel a(y) ~ (1/2pi) log|y| in the connection between the two vertices. Each height-h vertex contributes one factor that is asymptotically (c log|y| + d)/|y|^2 in the joint expansion, so the (h_1, h_2) correlation should be the product of two such factors at leading order, giving log^2|y|/|y|^4, which is the prediction. A rigorous route exists in principle: Kenyon-Wilson's formalism of spanning forests with connection constraints expresses the joint probability as an explicit finite combination of determinants of Green function derivatives with a line bundle (defect line) connection, and the asymptotics is a matter of expanding these determinants; what has been done for (0,h) by PGPR is exactly this expansion, so the (h_1,h_2) case is a longer version of the same computation with two defect lines. The genuine difficulty is bookkeeping and justification of the asymptotic expansion of a determinant of size growing with the number of nonlocal constraints, not a conceptual obstacle.
attempt.obstruction: The two-defect-line determinant expansion has not been carried out; the identification of the coefficient c_{h_1,h_2} with the LCFT prediction requires cancellations among terms of order log|y|/|y|^4 that are only visible after the full expansion.
attempt.key_identity: height h >= 1 probabilities are nonlocal functionals of the UST computable through spanning forests with a defect-line connection (Priezzhev; Kenyon-Wilson), and each nonlocal vertex carries a factor of the potential kernel a(y) ~ log|y|/(2 pi).

title: Almost sure finiteness of avalanches for the stationary sandpile on Z^2
statement: Open Question 6.7. Consider Z^2. Is it true that for nu-a.e. eta the configuration eta + 1_0 can be stabilised with finitely many topplings? (Here nu is the infinite-volume weak limit of the stationary sandpile measures. The source notes E_nu[n(o,x)] = lim_n G_n(o,x) = infinity for all x: on average every vertex topples infinitely often. On transient graphs, under the one-end assumption, avalanches are finite by Theorem 6.6.)
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 (sandpile Z^2 avalanches almost surely finite infinite volume). Every result found (Jarai-Redig 2008 for d >= 3; Jarai-Redig-Saada; Bhupatiraju-Hanson-Jarai 2017 on exponents) concerns d >= 3 or bounds in d = 2 without settling finiteness; the Codex tree's C0098 (Levine-Peres open problem on decidability of infinite toppling for i.i.d. initial sandpiles on Z^2) is a different question with a different initial law. Kept open.

attempt.method: Use the wave decomposition to reduce the question to two statements about the two-dimensional uniform spanning tree.
attempt.result: Adding a particle at o and toppling in waves, the k-th wave is finite iff the component of o in the k-th two-component spanning forest is finite; each wave, in the infinite-volume limit, corresponds to a bush (descendant set) of o in a uniform spanning tree of Z^2 (one-ended a.s., Pemantle), which is a.s. finite. So each individual wave is finite a.s.; the avalanche is finite iff the number of waves N = n(o,o) is finite. In d >= 3 E[N] = G(o,o) < infinity settles this (the source's Theorem 6.6). In d = 2 E[N] = infinity, so the question is exactly: is n(o,o) finite nu-a.s. even though its mean is infinite? Equivalently: after the k-th wave, o is unstable iff all four neighbours of o toppled in wave k, i.e. iff the k-th wave contains the whole neighbourhood of o. So the avalanche is infinite iff for every k the bush of o in the k-th forest contains all neighbours of o. Heuristically the waves form a Markov chain on configurations near o, and the event that the wave covers all neighbours of o has probability bounded away from 1 (a bush of o that misses at least one neighbour has positive probability in the USF of Z^2), which would make N geometric-like were the waves independent; they are not, and the conditional probability that the next wave covers the neighbourhood given the previous one did might tend to 1. A sufficient condition: nu(N = infinity) = 0 follows if inf over configurations reachable after a wave of the conditional probability that the next wave misses a neighbour of o is positive. The dichotomy E N = infinity but N < infinity a.s. is exactly what happens for the return-time structure of recurrent walks, and it is consistent with the exponent picture (F0030: tau <= 2 with E S_o = infinity).
attempt.obstruction: Successive waves are strongly dependent (each is a spanning-forest component conditioned on the previous configuration), and no uniform lower bound on the probability that a wave leaves a neighbour of o untoppled is known; the question is equivalent to recurrence-type behaviour of the wave chain at o with no tool to prove it.
attempt.key_identity: avalanche infinite iff every wave topples all four neighbours of o, i.e. n(o,o) = infinity; each wave is a.s. finite because the 2D USF is one-ended.

title: The bubble hypothesis for the backbone of the Brownian net
statement: Let N be the graph of the backbone of the Brownian net (paths started at time -infinity), S and M the sets of separation points and meeting points on N, S* = S union {(*,-infinity)}, M* = M union {(*,infinity)}, and phi: S* -> M*, phi(z) = the first meeting point of the left-most and right-most paths starting at z (phi(z) = (*,infinity) if they never meet), with phi: M* -> S* defined analogously by time reversal. Conjecture 8.1 (Bubble hypothesis) (a) Almost surely, there does not exist an infinite sequence of points (z_k)_{k>=0} in S* union M*, all different from each other, such that phi(z_{k-1}) = z_k for all k >= 1. (b) Almost surely, there does not exist an infinite sequence of points (z_k) in S* union M*, all different, such that phi(z_k) = z_{k-1} for all k >= 1.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 (Brownian net bubble hypothesis backbone fractal structure). Nothing addressing Conjecture 8.1 was found; the 2025 preprint 'Special times for the point set process of the Brownian net' (arXiv 2512.10761) concerns exceptional times of the branching-coalescing point set, not the phi-orbits. Kept open.

attempt.method: Translate the conjecture into a statement about the sizes of bubbles along a phi-orbit and give the scaling heuristic.
attempt.result: An infinite forward orbit z_0, z_1 = phi(z_0), ... consists of alternating separation and meeting points, each step passing from a separation point to the first meeting point of its left-most and right-most paths (the top of the bubble it opens), then from that meeting point, backwards in time, to the separation point where the two paths entering it last split (the bottom of the bubble containing it). Conjecture (a) says that this alternation of 'go to the top of my bubble, then to the bottom of the bubble I am the top of' terminates in a 2-cycle: the backbone's bubbles are nested finitely deeply in this sense. Scaling: a bubble opened at a separation point at time t has height (time duration) H with a heavy tail P(H > h) ~ c h^{-1/2} (the meeting time of the left-most and right-most paths of the net started at a separation point is the hitting time of zero by a difference process that is a Brownian motion with drift +2 pushed apart... the left-right paths drift away with speed 2 and meet only through the net's interaction, and the source's Section 3 gives the law of such excursions with infinite mean). The forward orbit produces a sequence of bubbles B_0 contained in? not nested: B_1 is the bubble whose top is the top of B_0's ... The key structural fact is that for z in S, phi(z) in M and phi(phi(z)) in S is the bottom of the bubble containing phi(z), and B_0 (bubble of z) is contained in the bubble of phi(phi(z)) unless they coincide; so the orbit is an increasing chain of bubbles B_0 subset B_2 subset B_4 ..., which terminates iff the chain of bubbles containing a given bubble is finite. Since the bubble containing a point of N at height scale h has height of order h times a random factor with infinite mean, and the backbone is stationary, the chain of containing bubbles of a given bubble is a renewal-type sequence of scales; it is infinite iff the scales stay bounded, and the conjecture (a) is the statement that the containing-bubble scales tend to infinity a.s., which follows if the chain of containing bubbles has a positive probability at each step of jumping to a bubble of comparable or larger height and no accumulation. The delicate case is accumulation at a finite point: infinitely many distinct bubbles containing B_0 all inside a bounded region, which would force infinitely many separation points in a bounded set with bubbles of non-decreasing size, contradicting local finiteness of relevant separation points only if all these bubbles are (-infinity, infinity)-relevant, which they need not be.
attempt.obstruction: The map phi is defined through the joint geometry of left-most and right-most paths, whose excursion structure has infinite mean, and no Markov property along a phi-orbit is available; the accumulation scenario (infinitely many nested bubbles in a bounded region) must be ruled out by a local finiteness statement finer than the known local finiteness of relevant separation points.
attempt.key_identity: B(z) subset B(phi^2(z)) for a separation point z: forward phi-orbits are increasing chains of bubbles.

title: Bubble complexity of the Brownian net backbone
statement: Assuming Conjecture 8.1(a), every separation or meeting point z on the backbone N has an orbit under phi that eventually 2-cycles; with n the smallest integer such that phi^{n+2}(z) = phi^n(z), z is of class I.n if phi^n(z) is (*,infinity) or (*,-infinity) and of class II.n if phi^n(z) is in R^2. Let C_{I,n}, resp. C_{II,n}, denote the set of meeting and separation points on N of class I.n, resp. II.n. Conjecture 8.2 (Bubble complexity): (a) The sets C_{II,0} and C_{II,1} are dense in N. (b) The sets C_{II,n} with n >= 2 and C_{I,n} with n >= 1 are locally finite subsets of R^2.
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08. Nothing found beyond the source. Kept open (and conditional on F0034 as the source states).

attempt.method: Give the dimension count behind (a) and (b).
attempt.result: Separation points of the Brownian net are dense in N and of Hausdorff dimension 1... more precisely the set of (p,pp)_s points has dimension 1 (Schertzer-Sun-Swart special points), and (-infinity, infinity)-relevant separation points are locally finite; class I.0 points are exactly the relevant separation points (phi(z) = (*,infinity)), class II.0 points are tops and bottoms of bubbles. Statement (a) says that bubbles and bubbles-inside-bubbles-with-one-crossover (class II.1) occur at all scales everywhere, which is plausible by scale invariance plus the fact that a bubble of any size contains, with probability bounded below, a sub-bubble whose left-right paths cross over once. Statement (b) says that a bubble whose internal crossover structure has depth n >= 2 is a macroscopic event: each additional level of the classification requires the left-most path of an inner bubble to reach the right-most path of the outer one, an event whose probability at scale ratio epsilon decays like a positive power epsilon^{a} (a two-sided exit for a Brownian excursion in a wedge), and local finiteness follows if a > the dimension of the ambient set of candidate points: for class II.n points, candidates are separation points (dimension 1 in the plane along the backbone... in space-time the set S has dimension 1) and the cost per level is a with a >= 1 would give local finiteness at n >= 2 provided the two levels' costs add, which is a Markov-type independence of the nested excursions. The exponent a is computable: the event that a bubble of height h contains a sub-bubble of height >= epsilon h whose left path crosses to the outer right path is the probability that two Brownian motions with drifts +-1 (the left-right pair) interact through a net path, of order epsilon^{1/2}... The count of class II.1 points at scale epsilon inside a unit bubble is then of order epsilon^{-1} * epsilon^{1/2} = epsilon^{-1/2} -> infinity, consistent with density in (a); at depth 2 the count is epsilon^{-1} epsilon^{1/2} epsilon^{1/2} = O(1), consistent with local finiteness in (b), if the crossover costs multiply. So the conjecture is exactly at the boundary predicted by the exponent 1/2, and its truth hinges on the independence of the two nested crossover events.
attempt.obstruction: The exponent 1/2 per crossover level is a heuristic from the drift of left-right paths, and the multiplicativity across nested levels needs a Markov property for nested bubbles that the Brownian net's branching structure does not obviously provide.
attempt.key_identity: expected number of depth-n points at scale epsilon in a unit bubble ~ epsilon^{-1 + n/2}: divergent for n <= 1, bounded for n >= 2.

title: Local finiteness of potential most recent common ancestors in the Brownian net
locator: Conjecture 8.3 (Potential most recent common ancestors), Section 8.2, PDF p. 72
statement: For the Brownian web, let M be the set of all first meeting points of pairs of paths started at time 0, M := {(x,t) in R^2: t > 0, exist pi, pi' in W({0} x R) with pi(t) = x = pi'(t), pi < pi' on (0,t)}, interpreted as most recent common ancestors; it is easy to see that M is a locally finite subset of R x (0, infinity). Conjecture 8.3 (Potential most recent common ancestors). If we replace W({0} x R) in (8.3) by N({0} x R), the set of all Brownian net paths started at time 0, then the set M is a locally finite subset of R x (0, infinity).
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08. Nothing found beyond the source. Kept open.

attempt.method: Compare the Brownian web argument with what changes when branching is allowed, and give the first-moment count.
attempt.result: In the Brownian web the paths started at time 0 form a coalescing system that is locally finite at every t > 0 (comes down from infinity), so meeting points in [a,b] x [s, infinity) are at most the number of paths alive at time s in a slightly larger interval, which is finite; local finiteness of M follows. In the Brownian net the set of paths started from {0} x R is not locally finite: the branching-coalescing point set xi_t started from R is a.s. locally finite for each t > 0 (it is Poisson with intensity 2 in stationarity), but the set of PATHS through a point is uncountable, and two net paths pi < pi' on (0,t) with pi(t) = pi'(t) can be created by branching arbitrarily close to t: take a net path, let it branch at a separation point at time t - epsilon into a left and a right path that meet again at time t (a bubble of height epsilon); the bubble's bottom and top would be a pair pi < pi' on (t - epsilon, t) meeting at t, but the definition requires pi < pi' on all of (0,t), which the two paths of a small bubble violate since they coincide before t - epsilon. So a PMRCA at (x,t) needs two net paths from time 0 that are disjoint on (0,t) and meet at t; the count is bounded by the number of pairs of points of xi_s (for any s in (0,t)) whose 'descendant sets' meet for the first time at (x,t). Since xi_s is locally finite, the number of such pairs in a compact set is finite provided each pair of points y < y' of xi_s produces only finitely many first-meeting points of net paths from y and from y' within a compact time window: the left-most path from y' and the right-most path from y determine the first possible meeting time T(y,y'), after which paths from y and y' can meet, and the set of first meeting points is contained in the set of meeting points of the net restricted to the strip between the right-most path from y and the left-most path from y' up to their meeting, which is a single point (their first meeting) plus possibly meeting points of intermediate paths that stayed disjoint: the intermediate paths are squeezed between the two extremal paths and are disjoint from both only before T(y,y'), so they meet the extremal ones... So the conjecture reduces to: for y < y' in xi_s, the first meeting points of pairs (pi from y, pi' from y') form a finite set, which holds if every such pair first meets at the meeting point of the right-most path from y and the left-most path from y' (a single point), which is false in general because an intermediate path pi from y can meet an intermediate path from y' before the extremal ones meet only if it crosses the right-most path from y, impossible by the left-right structure. Hence the first meeting of any pair from (y, y') occurs at the time when the right-most path from y meets the left-most path from y', at that unique point. Combined with local finiteness of xi_s and letting s -> 0 along a sequence, this gives local finiteness of M in R x [s, infinity) for each s > 0, i.e. the conjecture, provided the reduction's claim that intermediate paths cannot meet before the extremal ones is correct; the gap is that paths from y and y' need not be squeezed between the extremal paths from y and y' as stated (a path from y may go left of the left-most path from y? no, by definition it cannot), and I have not verified the treatment of pairs (pi, pi') where pi' starts at a point of xi_s that is a branching point with several net paths, nor whether 'first meeting' in the definition allows pi and pi' to touch without meeting.
attempt.obstruction: The reduction hinges on the claim that the first meeting point of any pair of net paths from two points y < y' is the meeting point of the right-most path from y and the left-most path from y'; this needs a proof that net paths from y' that are not the left-most cannot meet a path from y earlier, and the fine structure at separation points (paths that coincide then split) must be handled.
attempt.key_identity: a pair (pi from y, pi' from y') with pi < pi' can meet no earlier than the right-most path from y meets the left-most path from y'.
attempt.independent_check: The argument was not checked against the paths-topology definition of 'pi < pi' on (0,t)' and should be treated as a sketch.

title: Tracy-Widom fluctuations for the Howitt-Warren flow
statement: '(4) For the Howitt-Warren flow (K^up_{s,t}(x, dy))_{s<t, x in R} introduced in Section 5.1, which gives the transition probability kernels of a random motion in a continuum space-time random environment constructed from the Brownian web and net, can one show that for any x in R, -log K^up_{0,t}(0, [tx, tx+1]) has Tracy-Widom GUE fluctuations on the scale t^{1/3} as t -> infinity, similar to recent results in [Barraquand-Corwin 2015] for random walks on Z in special i.i.d. Beta-distributed space-time random environments?'
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08. Barraquand and Rychnovsky, 'Large deviations for sticky Brownian motions' (2019/2020) prove Tracy-Widom GUE fluctuations for a specific Howitt-Warren flow (the uniform sticky/Bethe-ansatz-solvable case) in the large-deviation regime of the kernel, and Yu (2016, 'Edwards-Wilkinson fluctuations in the Howitt-Warren flows') shows Gaussian t^{1/4} fluctuations for the dual smoothing process. So the question is answered for one characteristic measure and for the large-deviation regime; for general Howitt-Warren flows (arbitrary characteristic measure nu) it is open. Admitted with that residual.

attempt.method: State the exact solvability boundary and what universality would require.
attempt.result: Barraquand-Rychnovsky's result uses the Bethe ansatz for sticky Brownian motions with a specific interaction (the uniform Howitt-Warren flow, the continuum limit of the Beta random walk in random environment), giving an exact Fredholm determinant for the moments of the kernel; the t^{1/3} Tracy-Widom fluctuations of -log K_{0,t}(0, [tx, tx+1]) for x in the large-deviation range follow. For a general characteristic measure nu the sticky interaction is not integrable and the question becomes a KPZ universality statement for a random walk in a continuum space-time random environment; the Howitt-Warren flow with characteristic measure nu is the scaling limit of RWRE with i.i.d. environment whose law is determined by nu, and the conjecture is that the quenched large-deviation fluctuations belong to the KPZ class regardless of nu. This is the continuum analogue of the (open) universality conjecture for the Beta RWRE among space-time random walks in random environment, for which the only rigorous KPZ results are integrable (Beta, Barraquand-Corwin) and the general case is expected but unproven. A partial reduction: by the source's Section 5 the Howitt-Warren flow is a function of the Brownian net plus marks, so the question is a statement about the Brownian net alone; Yu's Edwards-Wilkinson t^{1/4} result shows that the moderate-deviation regime is Gaussian, so Tracy-Widom can only appear in the large-deviation regime |x| bounded away from 0 on the diffusive scale, i.e. the question as literally stated (fixed x, window [tx, tx+1]) is in the large-deviation regime for x != 0 and the answer is expected to be yes; for x = 0 the fluctuations are of a different (Gaussian, t^{1/4}) nature by Yu, so the question's 'any x' must be read as x != 0.
attempt.obstruction: Outside the Bethe-ansatz-solvable characteristic measure there is no exact formula, and no non-integrable proof of Tracy-Widom fluctuations exists for any RWRE-type model.
attempt.key_identity: the uniform Howitt-Warren flow is the continuum limit of the Beta random walk in random environment, the integrable case.

title: Maximal noise structure of the Brownian web and the factorisation set
statement: '(6) The Brownian web has been shown by Ellis and Feldheim to be a two-dimensional black noise, equipped with a family of sub-sigma-fields indexed by finite unions of open rectangles in R^2. Is there a maximal extension of the family of sub-sigma-fields, indexed by a Boolean algebra of domains in R^2 that include the rectangles, such that the Brownian web remains a noise? A similar question is also open for the scaling limit of critical planar percolation. Recently Tsirelson showed by general arguments that there exists some continuous path f starting at time -infinity, such that F_{f-} and F_{f+}, the sigma-fields generated by Brownian web paths restricted respectively to the left or the right of the graph of f, do not jointly generate the full sigma-field F. Can we characterize the set of f for which the factorization property F = F_{f-} v F_{f+} holds? (The case f = 0 has been treated by Ellis-Feldheim.)'
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 (Brownian web black noise factorization Tsirelson Ellis Feldheim). Nothing beyond the cited works found; the campaign already holds Tsirelson's 2003 noise paper as a source (tsirelson_noise_2003, unmined in intake D). Kept open.

attempt.method: Give the natural candidate for the factorisation set and the mechanism that makes Tsirelson's counterexample work.
attempt.result: Factorisation F = F_{f-} v F_{f+} says the web is determined by its restrictions to the two sides of the graph of f. For f = 0 (a vertical line in space-time: x = 0) Ellis-Feldheim prove it; for a horizontal line (a fixed time) factorisation is the Markov property, which holds. For a general curve f, consider the Brownian web paths that cross the graph of f: a path restricted to one side is known up to its crossing times; the web is recovered if the crossings of f by web paths can be matched across the curve, which requires that the set of crossing points is 'visible' from both sides. Tsirelson's obstruction is measure-theoretic: for a black noise, sub-sigma-fields of domains with rough boundary need not generate; a continuous f whose graph has positive area?... a continuous path f cannot have positive-area graph, but the crossing set of a rough f by the web can be uncountable with points where paths touch f without crossing, and the information 'which touching point continues to which path' is lost on each side. Candidate characterisation: factorisation holds iff the graph of f is a.s. crossed by the web's paths only at a locally finite set of points on each compact time interval... but web paths from every point cross any curve transversal to time infinitely often near a point where f is not Lipschitz. The natural conjecture: factorisation holds for f of locally bounded variation (or Lipschitz) and fails for f rougher than Brownian; the threshold should be Holder-1/2, since a Brownian-type f can be 'followed' by web paths (a web path and an independent Brownian f meet on a set of positive dimension, and the web has (1,2) points at which two paths separate, which a rough f can pass between). This gives a precise conjecture to test: factorisation holds iff the set of (1,2)-points of the web lying on the graph of f is a.s. empty, which is automatic for f Lipschitz (the (1,2)-points form a dimension-3/2 set in space-time whose intersection with a Lipschitz graph is a.s. empty since 3/2 + 1 < 2 + 1... dimension count 3/2 + 1 - 2 = 1/2 > 0, so not automatic; the correct count uses the parabolic scaling of the web).
attempt.obstruction: There is no general criterion for the factorisation property of black noises along curves; the parabolic dimension count for the (1,2)-points on a curve gives a plausible threshold but no proof in either direction.
attempt.key_identity: factorisation along f requires that crossings of f by web paths be recoverable from each side, which fails at (1,2)-points on the graph of f.

title: Scaling limit of critical and near-critical oriented percolation in 1+1 dimensions
statement: '(8) The Brownian web appears in the scaling limit of super-critical oriented percolation, as discussed in Section 7.2.6, and the Brownian net is expected to arise if the percolation parameter p is allowed to vary in a small interval. However, the most interesting question is: What is the scaling limit of critical (and near-critical) oriented percolation (OP) on Z^{1+1}? The Brownian net with killing provides a simpler model to study the OP universality class. We expect that in the near-critical scaling limit, one would obtain a family of models which interpolates between the Brownian net and the scaling limit of critical oriented percolation. However, such a goal appears far out of reach at the moment, because there are no conjectures at all on what the critical scaling limit might be, and neither have critical exponents been shown to exist.'
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 and the campaign's own ledgers. The existing rows on oriented percolation (C0078 mean-field behaviour for d > 4, C0126 random walk on the IIC in d = 5, 6, P0219 the Hammersley flow) do not state the 1+1 dimensional scaling limit; no rigorous scaling limit or exponent existence for 1+1 critical OP (directed percolation universality class) was found. Kept open.

attempt.method: State what is known rigorously at criticality in 1+1 dimensions and why the problem is harder than undirected planar percolation.
attempt.result: Known: p_c exists, theta(p_c) = 0 (Bezuidenhout-Grimmett), the correlation length diverges at p_c with exponential decay below p_c, and the critical exponents (beta = 0.2765, nu_parallel = 1.7338, nu_perp = 1.0969 from numerics) are believed universal but have no closed form and no rigorous existence proof; directed percolation is not conformally invariant (time and space scale differently, with dynamical exponent z = nu_par/nu_perp = 1.58), so the SLE/CLE machinery that solved undirected 2D percolation has no analogue. The Brownian net is the scaling limit of oriented percolation in the supercritical regime p -> 1 with branching rate scaled (Sun-Swart), i.e. it is the p -> 1 corner of the phase diagram, not the critical point. Any candidate for the critical scaling limit must be a random closed subset of space-time invariant under the anisotropic scaling (x, t) -> (a x, a^z t) with z = 1.58 (non-integer), which rules out every known continuum object built from Brownian motion (z = 2) or from conformal invariance (z = 1). One structural statement that is provable: if the critical exponents nu_perp, nu_par exist and the family of near-critical models is tight under anisotropic scaling, then subsequential limits exist by compactness in the Schramm-Smirnov quad-crossing topology adapted to oriented crossings; uniqueness would need a characterisation, and no candidate characterisation (an analogue of Cardy's formula) exists. So the reduction is: the problem is at the stage undirected planar percolation was before Cardy/Schramm, minus conformal invariance.
attempt.obstruction: No integrable or conformal structure is available for directed percolation; existence of exponents would already need a scaling relation argument for a non-isotropic model, and the near-critical interpolation with the Brownian net presupposes the critical object.
attempt.key_identity: anisotropic scaling invariance (x,t) -> (a x, a^{z} t) with z = nu_par/nu_perp = 1.58 (numerical) for any critical limit.
attempt.independent_check: The numerical exponent values are from the physics literature (Hinrichsen's review), quoted from memory.
